newsitem.title: UK: U.S. tobacco accord has worldwide implications.
newsitem.headline: U.S. tobacco accord has worldwide implications.

text.p: An admission by an American tobacco company that cigarettes are addictive and cause cancer will have far-reaching implications well beyond the United States, legal experts said on Friday.

Martyn Day, who is representing 23 lung cancer sufferers in Britain's first class-action suit against two tobacco companies on a no-win, no fee basis, said the move by the Liggett Group in the United States could result in a flood of legal actions.

"The tobacco companies on both sides of the Atlantic have built this facade of refusing to accept that their products cause harm, refusing to accept the addictive nature of cigarettes," he told BBC radio.
"The fact that Liggett is now openly accepting that that is untrue I think is a very major change for us in these cases."

Liggett, which is owned by Bennett LeBow's Brooke Group Ltd., agreed on Thursday to settle with the attorney generals of 22 states who have sued the industry to recoup the Medicaid health care costs of treating smokers.
"It could be dynamite for litigants all over the world," Dr Julian Fulbrook, a lecturer in law at the London School of Economics and a personal injury expert, told Reuters.

"Because the tobacco industry has always been a transitional business, information has been shared around in the tobacco world, so almost certainly the knowledge about the scientific and medical factors in the United States will be common knowledge to tobacco producers worldwide. That is going to be pretty important to see how that plays out."

Describing the Liggett settlement as a "breakthrough," Fulbrook said it could pave the way from U.S. states suing tobacco companies to individual, private litigation. It will also give new impetus to stalled cases around the world. "There's going to be a logjam (of cases) suddenly bursting," he added.

The U.S. settlement could be particularly important for Day's clients who are suing Imperial Tobacco and Gallaher, which have 80 percent of the British market, for failing to change their product to limit the dangers of smoking.
"It could be overwhelming important if the British litigants and their lawyers can get their hands on some of the written material," said Fulbrook.

Day's case is based on the claim that the tobacco companies, makers of Benson and Hedges, Silk Cut and Embassy brands, were aware in the 1950s that their products were addictive and killing large numbers of their consumers.
Day alleged that they were aware that it was the tar that was the primary cause of death.

"We said that if they had acknowledged that openly at the time they could have taken steps, particularly by reducing the tar, to make sure that the number of people contracting lung cancer were vastly reduced," he said.
"We're feeling much encouraged by the news today," he added.

Two cases are also pending in France against tobacco monopoly Seita. In the southern city of Bexiers, the family of a young woman who died of lung cancer last October is seeking more than a million francs ($175,000) in damages.
It alleges that the firm sold an "inherently dangerous" product due to its addictive nature and its link to cancer.
In an earlier suit, a two-pack-a-day smoker of Seita's Gauloises Brunes has accused the company of causing his cancer and is seeking 2.7 million francs ($473,000) in damages.
Experts say that now that one tobacco company has admitted the health hazards of cigarettes, it will be difficult for others to continue denying it.
"I think it is going to be impossible," said Fulbrook.

In addition to the civil suits, the Liggett case opens up the possibility of potential criminal charges against the tobacco company executives who have sworn under oath before government committees in the United States that smoking is not addictive. ($ = 5.704 French Francs)
